tagline: Read each piece silently. Look away, say it back in your own words, and react to it. Once you finish the stimulus, say the whole argument back from memory.
task: Read each piece silently. Look away, say it back in your own words, then give it a reaction. After the final piece, press space. The stimulus disappears, and you recall the whole argument out loud from memory.
rules: Read each piece silently. Everything you say back, including your reaction and final recall, is out loud.
Read about a sentence at a time. When you are unsure how much to take on, take less.
Look away from the screen and say it back in your own words, like you are telling a friend what it said.
Then colour it: react to that specific piece with a thought, question, doubt, example, joke, or feeling.
Repeat these steps through the whole stimulus.
After the final piece, press space. The stimulus disappears and stays gone. Say the entire argument back from memory, with every detail you can still hold.
Press space again to move on. The whole section records in one take, with no pauses or breaks.

briefing.lede: Read these instructions once before your first section. After that, come back when you need a reminder.

sections.heading: You can understand every sentence and still reach the answers remembering almost none of it.
body: You can follow a stimulus sentence by sentence and understand every part. Then you reach answer choice C and realise you are holding almost none of it. That is not a comprehension problem. It is a retention problem, and that is what this drill trains.
Understanding is necessary for everything and sufficient for nothing. Understanding the stimulus is not enough if it is gone by the time you reach the answers.

Most everyday reading trains you to reach the end, not retain every detail. You scan names, drop connecting words, and turn a list of three things into one vague label. That works for a phone bill. It does not work for the LSAT.

sections.heading: How the method works
body: For each piece, read it, say it back, and colour it. Once you finish the stimulus, recall the whole argument. You decide how much to read at a time, and nothing on the screen decides for you.

Space is the only key, and you press it twice per stimulus. The first press takes the text away and asks you for the whole argument from memory. The second press moves you to the next stimulus. Nothing advances on its own, so a pause to think costs you nothing but the clock.

steps.label: Read it
steps.body: Read about a sentence silently. Give every word enough attention to hear the sentence naturally in your head. When you are unsure how much to take on, take less. If you take on too much, the beginning is usually what disappears first.

steps.label: Tell it back
steps.body: Look away from the screen and say it back in your own words, like you are telling a friend what it said. Out of order is fine. Casual is fine. Laughing is fine.

steps.label: Colour it
steps.body: React to what you just said. Give it a thought, question, doubt, example, joke, or feeling. Keep it short, but make it specific. If the same reaction could fit any sentence, it does not count.

steps.label: Recall it
steps.body: After the final piece, press space. The stimulus disappears and does not come back. Say the entire argument out loud from memory, with every detail you can still hold. This is what gets scored.

sections.heading: Simpler is not the same as shorter
body: Do not give back only the gist or what seemed important. You cannot know which details will matter until you have read the whole stimulus. Filtering as you read is how useful information disappears.
Fewer words is fine when the words cover the same ideas. Fewer ideas is not. Names, numbers, and small words carrying the load, such as all, most, only, and probably, have to come back too.
**Being efficient does not mean leaving information out.**

sections.heading: When nothing comes to mind
body: You may try to colour a sentence and find that nothing comes to mind. Usually, the hidden thought is that nothing feels good enough to say.

Do not judge the reaction before you say it. Say something obvious on purpose if you have to. "Okay, sure." "That seems like a stretch." "Who measured that?" All of those count when they connect to what you just read.
The reaction makes the sentence yours instead of the author's. Skip it and you are back to repeating words you do not own.

sections.heading: Look away from the text
body: The text stays visible while you say each piece back. You have to look away from it yourself.
If you read while you recall, you stop using your short-term memory and slide back into the author's exact words. Looking away forces you to rebuild the meaning in your own words.
This is also the version that works on paper and on test day.

sections.heading: Build toward twenty-five minutes
body: The goal is twenty-five minutes for a whole section. It only counts when you read every stimulus, say each piece back, colour it, and recall the whole argument. Finishing early by skipping parts is not finishing early. If you receive extra time on test day, use your full allotted time here too.
The clock counts up so you can track your pace without watching your time disappear.
Do the method correctly before you try to do it quickly. Go slower while it is new. Speed follows once the method becomes automatic.

briefing.closer: One section keeps the method steady. Improvement starts with the second.

coach.drill: a whole Logical Reasoning section run out loud, where the student reads each line of a stimulus, looks away, tells it back from memory in her own words, reacts to it, and gives The Recall of the whole stimulus before moving to the next one
rubric: Judge by meaning, never by wording. Her own words are required here, so a good recall will never match the line's phrasing. High overlap with the original is the failure, not the standard.
Order is free. She is encouraged to deliver the ideas out of the order she read them in, and reordering must never cost her anything.
Casual, unpolished, laughing delivery is expected. Never mark down for style, length or fluency.
A detail merely gestured at is not carried. Naming the topic is not the same as saying what was claimed about it.
Numbers, names, dates, quantities and connecting words are each their own detail. Never treat one as carried because the sentence around it was.
A reaction that could be pasted onto any other sentence does not count as a colour. Judge whether it engages this content, never whether it is correct or well put.
Score The Recall against the captured key for that stimulus, not against a retelling. A different name for the same move is fine; missing the move is not.
Silence during a silent read is correct and expected. Only silence inside a recall or a colour counts against her.
coach.partial_rule: Mark 'partial' when the retelling is real but at least one detail went missing, which is the drill's ordinary state. Mark 'incorrect' only when the response is a gist or a topic label rather than a retelling.
